title: Architecture-to-Landscape Transferability of U-Net Variants and Morphology-Aware Urban Sprawl Mapping in Heterogeneous Cities
content: Urban land-cover models are often compared as though one architecture should dominate across cities, yet the spatial organization of water, vegetation, Built-up surfaces, and exposed or transitional land varies substantially among urban landscapes. We evaluated four pretrained U-Net variants, Base U-Net, Attention U-Net, Self-Attention U-Net, and a depth-split Hybrid U-Net, using the same six-channel Sentinel-2 Level-2A input composed of B02, B03, B04, B08, normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), and normalized difference water index (NDWI). Macro F1, the unweighted mean of the four class-specific F1 scores, was predeclared as the sole primary ranking criterion across eight U.S. evaluation cities, while overall accuracy, balanced accuracy, class-level F1, Built-up F1, intersection over union (IoU), and confusion matrices were retained as diagnostics. All image variant results performed differently which  supports a landscape-dependent architecture framework rather than universal framework. The city of New Orleans was used as a case study to evaluate the Built-up change by using independently assessed 2015 and 2026 masks, each with a Built-up score (F1=0.953). Pixel-wise comparison identified 16.7484 km² of gross Built-up gain, 6.8835 km² of loss, and a net increase of 9.8649 km². Landscape Expansion Index analysis classified the gain primarily as edge-expansion (51.01%), followed by infill (43.74%) and outlying growth (5.25%), with the ranking stable across 10-50 m neighborhood sensitivity and a 0.05 ha minimum mapping unit test. Four CNN-image-variant architectures were evaluated within a consistent Sentinel-2 framework across eight U.S. cities and by applying the resulting mapping outputs to a new test site (New Orleans), we modeled the relationship between the CNN-image-variant architecture, landscape, and urban sprawl patterns. Results from the study may inform CNN and GeoAI researchers, urban planners and practitioners in the choice of CNN-image-variants and changes in urban sprawl patterns.
